config.title: CSS Modules

intro.title: CSS Modules
intro.body: In this lesson, you'll build a simple profile card component using CSS Modules to style it. You'll learn how CSS Modules work by creating scoped CSS classes that only apply to specific React components, preventing style conflicts. The main technologies involved are React with TypeScript, CSS Modules syntax, and the module system for importing styles. You'll practice creating separate CSS files for components and applying those styles in a type-safe way. By the end, you'll understand how to organize component styles locally while maintaining clean, maintainable code.
intro.usecase: CSS Modules are essential for building scalable, maintainable UI components in large React applications like e-commerce platforms, SaaS dashboards, and content management systems. You'll use them to style reusable components such as product cards, data tables, navigation menus, and modal dialogs without worrying about CSS class name collisions. This approach is particularly valuable when multiple developers work on the same codebase, ensuring component styles remain isolated and predictable. For example, a dashboard with multiple filter panels and data visualization widgets can use CSS Modules to keep each component's styles self-contained while maintaining consistent design tokens.

objectives: Apply CSS Modules to create scoped styles that prevent naming conflicts in React components.
Implement CSS Modules by importing style objects from .module.css files into TypeScript components.
Use TypeScript interfaces to define type-safe props for components that receive CSS class names.
Assign CSS class names to JSX elements by accessing properties from the imported style object.
Construct CSS Modules files with standard CSS syntax to define component-specific styles.
Utilize CSS Modules to apply multiple class names to a single element using template literals or array joins.
Execute conditional class name application based on component state or props using CSS Modules.
Define and use CSS custom properties (variables) within CSS Modules for consistent theming.
Access nested CSS selectors within CSS Modules to style child elements without global conflicts.
Modify existing React components to replace global CSS with scoped CSS Modules implementation.
Control CSS specificity by leveraging the automatic scoping provided by CSS Modules.
Implement responsive design patterns within CSS Modules using media queries and scoped selectors.

steps.title: Initialize state with useState
steps.instruction: Inside your component, initialize a state variable named 'isActive' using the useState hook with a boolean type and an initial value of false.
steps.hint: Remember to import useState from 'react' if you haven't already. Use TypeScript generics to specify the boolean type.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component should have a state variable 'isActive' initialized with useState<boolean>(false).
successCriteria: useState imported
isActive state variable declared
TypeScript boolean type specified
Initial value set to false
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the isActive state variable with the correct TypeScript type and initial value.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've: 1) Used useState with the boolean type, 2) Named the variable 'isActive', 3) Set the initial value to false.
steps.feedbackWrong: The state initialization isn't quite right. Remember to use useState<boolean>(false) to create an isActive state variable.

steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a handleToggle function that can toggle the isActive state between true and false.
successCriteria: The code should include a function named handleToggle that calls setIsActive with the opposite of the current isActive value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a toggle handler function that will modify the isActive state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function is named handleToggle and properly toggles the isActive state value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The toggle handler function isn't quite right. Remember to create a function named handleToggle that calls setIsActive with the opposite of the current isActive value.

steps.instruction: Add a className attribute to the wrapper <div> element to apply the CSS module class. Use the syntax className={styles.container}.
steps.hint: The styles object is imported from the CSS module file. Access the 'container' class property on it.

steps.title: Add button with CSS module class
steps.instruction: Add a button element inside the return statement, after the paragraph. Give it a CSS module class using className={styles.button} and set its text content to 'Toggle State'.
steps.hint: Add a <button> tag with the className attribute set to styles.button and the text 'Toggle State' between the tags.

<button className={styles.button}>Click me</button>

successCriteria: The button element must be present in the JSX, have className={styles.button}, and contain the text 'Toggle State'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a button with a CSS module class. This demonstrates how CSS Modules can style interactive elements while keeping styles scoped to the component.

steps.title: Wire button click to handler
steps.instruction: Add an onClick attribute to the button element and set it to call the handleToggle function when clicked.
steps.hint: Use the onClick prop on the button element and pass the handleToggle function reference.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of wiring a button click to a handler
<button onClick={handleToggle}>Toggle</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The button will be wired to the toggle handler, but the handler function itself is not yet defined (that will be added in the next step).
successCriteria: The button element has an onClick attribute
The onClick attribute value is {handleToggle}
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully wired the button's click event to the handler function. The button is now ready to trigger the toggle functionality.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the onClick wiring isn't quite complete. Make sure you're using the exact handler function name 'handleToggle' without calling it (no parentheses).
steps.feedbackWrong: The button click isn't properly wired to the handler. Remember to add an onClick attribute to the button element and set it to {handleToggle}.

steps.title: Conditional CSS module class
steps.instruction: Add a conditional CSS module class to the button's className using a template literal. Use the pattern `${styles.button} ${isActive ? styles.active : ''}` to apply the 'active' class only when isActive is true.
steps.hint: Update the button's className attribute to include both the base 'button' class and conditionally add the 'active' class based on the isActive state.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of conditional CSS module class
<button className={`${styles.button} ${isActive ? styles.active : ''}`}>
  Click me
</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The button will have a conditional CSS module class that adds the 'active' style when isActive is true.
successCriteria: Update the button's className attribute
Use template literal syntax with backticks
Include styles.button as base class
Add conditional styles.active when isActive is true
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a conditional CSS module class to the button. The 'active' class will now be applied only when the isActive state is true.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check the syntax. Make sure you're using a template literal with backticks (`) and including both the base 'button' class and the conditional 'active' class.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional CSS module class wasn't added correctly. Review the template literal syntax and ensure you're conditionally applying the 'active' class based on the isActive state.

steps.title: Display state in UI
steps.instruction: Update the button text to show the current state by using a ternary expression inside the button content. Display 'Active' when isActive is true and 'Inactive' when false.
steps.hint: Inside the button element, replace the static text with a ternary expression that checks isActive: {isActive ? 'Active' : 'Inactive'}
steps.expectedOutcome: The button text will dynamically change between 'Active' and 'Inactive' when clicked, reflecting the current isActive state.
successCriteria: The button element must contain a ternary expression that uses the isActive state variable to conditionally render 'Active' or 'Inactive' text.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully made the button text reflect the current state. The ternary expression dynamically updates the UI based on isActive.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using a ternary expression with isActive inside the button content. Check that you're displaying 'Active' when true and 'Inactive' when false.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button text should change based on the isActive state. Try using a ternary expression like {isActive ? 'Active' : 'Inactive'} inside the button element.
